          text        The rapid adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) has intensified the need for accurate energy consumption prediction models tobrsupport intelligent transportation systems, battery management, route planning, and charging infrastructure optimization. Traditionalbrdata-driven approaches often rely solely on historical vehicle telemetry and overlook the underlying physical principles governingbrvehicle dynamics. Furthermore, centralized machine learning frameworks require the collection of raw data from multiple sources,brraising concerns regarding privacy, scalability, and data ownership. To address these limitations, this study proposes a Physics-brInformed Federated Learning Framework for Electric Vehicle Energy Consumption Prediction with Real-Time Traffic Simulation.br       The proposed framework integrates vehicle telemetry, battery characteristics, environmental conditions, and road attributesbrwith physics-based power estimation features derived from aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance, grade resistance, and inertialbrforces. These engineered features are combined with a Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) regression model to improvebrpredictive accuracy. A federated learning architecture is further incorporated to enable privacy-preserving distributed model trainingbracross multiple vehicle groups without requiring the exchange of raw data. The experimental dataset consists of 5,000 electricbrvehicle operational records containing driving behavior, battery parameters, weather conditions, and trip-level information. Tobrevaluate the contribution of different feature sets, four predictive configurations are investigated, including raw-feature learning,brreduced-feature learning, physics-only learning, and hybrid physics-informed learning.br       Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid physics-informed model achieves the best performance with a MeanbrAbsolute Error (MAE) of 0.4629 kWh, a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.5744 kWh, and an Rspan style=font-size 0.667em;2span score of 0.9320, significantlybroutperforming physics-only and reduced-feature baselines. The federated implementation achieves a comparable MAE of 0.4844brkWh, indicating that privacy-preserving distributed learning can be achieved with minimal loss in predictive performance. Tobrdemonstrate real-world applicability, the trained model is integrated with the Simulation of Urban Mobility (SUMO) platformbrfor real-time vehicle energy prediction and visualization. An interactive analytics dashboard is also developed to provide modelbrevaluation, performance monitoring, and vehicle-level insights.br       The findings indicate that combining physics-informed feature engineering with federated machine learning offers an effectivebrand scalable solution for accurate EV energy consumption prediction while maintaining data privacy. The proposed frameworkbrprovides a practical foundation for next-generation intelligent transportation systems, smart charging infrastructure, and large-scalebrEV fleet management applications.br       Keywords—  Electric Vehicle Energy Consumption Prediction, Physics-Informed Machine Learning, Federated Learning,brLightGBM, Intelligent Transportation Systems, SUMO Traffic Simulation, Privacy-Preserving Learning, Energy Analytics.,

          text     The global transportation sector is undergoing a significant transformation driven by the rapid adoption of electric vehiclesn(EVs). Growing concerns regarding greenhouse gas emissions, climate change, fossil fuel dependency, and urban air pollutionnhave accelerated the transition from conventional internal combustion engine vehicles to electrified transportation systems.nGovernments, industries, and research organizations worldwide are actively promoting EV deployment through regulatorynpolicies, financial incentives, and investments in charging infrastructure. Consequently, electric vehicles have emerged as a keyntechnological solution for achieving sustainable mobility and reducing the environmental impact of transportation systems.n    Despite these advantages, several operational challenges continue to hinder large-scale EV adoption. One of the mostncritical challenges is the accurate estimation and prediction of vehicle energy consumption. Unlike conventional vehicles,nwhose refueling process is relatively fast and predictable, EV performance is strongly influenced by battery capacity, drivingnbehavior, traffic conditions, environmental factors, road characteristics, and vehicle dynamics. Inaccurate estimation of energynconsumption may lead to range anxiety, inefficient charging schedules, suboptimal route planning, and increased operationalncosts for fleet operators.n    Accurate energy consumption prediction plays a vital role in numerous EV-related applications, including battery managementnsystems, intelligent navigation, charging station recommendation systems, fleet energy optimization, and smart grid integration.nReliable prediction models enable vehicle operators and transportation authorities to estimate future energy requirements,noptimize charging infrastructure utilization, and improve overall transportation efficiency.           text     Predicting EV energy consumption is a complex problem due to the multidimensional interactions among vehicle, driver,nenvironmental, and infrastructure-related factors. Energy consumption is influenced by vehicle speed, acceleration patterns,nroad gradients, battery characteristics, ambient temperature, wind conditions, traffic congestion, tire pressure, and vehicle mass.nThese variables often exhibit nonlinear relationships that are difficult to capture using traditional analytical approaches.n    Conventional physics-based models estimate energy consumption using vehicle dynamics equations and power balancenformulations. Although these models provide interpretability and physical consistency, they often require accurate parameterncalibration and may struggle to represent complex real-world driving conditions. In contrast, data-driven machine learningnapproaches can capture nonlinear relationships directly from historical data but frequently lack physical interpretability andnmay exhibit poor generalization outside the observed data distribution.n    Another major challenge arises from data privacy and ownership concerns. Modern EVs continuously generate largenvolumes of telemetry data containing detailed information about driving behavior, battery usage, and travel patterns. Traditionalncentralized machine learning approaches require collecting and aggregating this data in a central repository, which introducesnconcerns related to privacy, cybersecurity, data governance, and regulatory compliance. These challenges become particularlynsignificant in large-scale fleet management systems where data originates from multiple geographically distributed sources.n    Therefore, there is a growing need for predictive frameworks that simultaneously provide high prediction accuracy, physicalninterpretability, scalability, and privacy preservation.,

          text     Recent advancements in machine learning have significantly improved the accuracy of EV energy consumption predictionnmodels. Various regression algorithms, including Random Forest, Support Vector Regression, Gradient Boosting Machines,nXGBoost, and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), have demonstrated strong predictive capabilities across diversentransportation datasets. Deep learning techniques such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, Gated Recurrent Unitsn(GRU), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Transformer-based architectures have further expanded the ability to modelncomplex temporal dependencies in vehicle operational data.n    While these approaches have achieved promising results, many existing studies rely exclusively on raw sensor measurementsnand historical observations. Such models often treat the prediction process as a purely statistical problem, ignoring thenfundamental physical mechanisms that govern vehicle energy consumption. As a result, prediction performance may degradenwhen models encounter driving scenarios that differ from those represented in the training dataset.n    To address these limitations, researchers have increasingly explored Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML), whichnintegrates domain knowledge and physical equations into data-driven learning frameworks. By incorporating physically mean-ningful variables such as aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance, grade resistance, and inertial power, PIML models can improvenprediction accuracy while maintaining consistency with established vehicle dynamics principles.,

          text     Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for distributed machine learning in privacy-sensitive envi-nronments. Unlike centralized learning approaches, federated learning enables model training across multiple clients withoutnrequiring the exchange of raw data. Instead, each client performs local training and shares model updates or predictions, therebynpreserving data privacy while facilitating collaborative learning.n    The application of federated learning within intelligent transportation systems has gained considerable attention in recentnyears. Vehicle manufacturers, fleet operators, and transportation agencies increasingly seek methods for leveraging distributedndata sources while complying with privacy regulations and organizational data-sharing constraints. Federated learning offers anpractical solution by enabling decentralized model development across geographically distributed vehicles and transportationnnetworks.n    Despite the growing interest in federated learning, relatively few studies have investigated its integration with physics-ninformed EV energy prediction frameworks. Existing research often focuses on either privacy-preserving learning or energynprediction independently, leaving a significant opportunity to combine these complementary approaches into a unified frame-nwork.,

The highly nonlinear interactions among these variables make energy predictionna challenging problem and have motivated researchers to develop increasingly sophisticated prediction methodologies.n    Over the past decade, research in EV energy prediction has evolved from traditional analytical approaches toward advancednmachine learning and artificial intelligence frameworks. Early studies primarily relied on vehicle dynamics equations andnphysical models to estimate energy demand. Although these methods provided interpretability and consistency with establishednengineering principles, they often struggled to capture the complexity of real-world driving environments. The availability ofnlarge-scale vehicle telemetry datasets subsequently enabled the adoption of data-driven machine learning approaches capable ofnlearning predictive patterns directly from operational data. More recently, researchers have begun exploring hybrid approachesnthat combine physical knowledge with machine learning techniques, aiming to achieve both predictive accuracy and physicalnconsistency.n    The evolution of EV energy prediction methodologies reflects a broader transition occurring across intelligent transportationnsystems, where purely analytical models are increasingly being complemented by data-driven approaches capable of adaptingnto complex and dynamic environments.,

          text     Physics-based energy consumption models constitute the foundation of electric vehicle energy analysis. These approachesnestimate vehicle energy demand by explicitly modeling the physical forces that influence vehicle motion. Such models arenderived from classical vehicle dynamics and energy balance principles and provide a direct mathematical relationship betweennvehicle operation and energy consumption.n    The most commonly modeled forces include aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance, grade resistance, and inertial forces.nAerodynamic drag becomes increasingly important at higher vehicle speeds and represents the resistance generated by airflownaround the vehicle body. Rolling resistance results from tire deformation and road surface interaction, while grade resistancencaptures the impact of road inclines and declines. Inertial forces represent the energy required to accelerate or decelerate thenvehicle.n    Physics-based models have several advantages. Their outputs can be directly interpreted in terms of known engineeringnprinciples, making them attractive for battery management systems and energy optimization applications. Furthermore, thesenmodels often require relatively small amounts of data compared with machine learning approaches and can be implementednefficiently in embedded systems.n    However, the predictive performance of purely physics-based methods depends heavily on accurate parameter estimation.nVariables such as drag coefficients, tire conditions, vehicle loading, environmental factors, and battery efficiency may varynsignificantly under real-world operating conditions. Small inaccuracies in these parameters can result in substantial predictionnerrors. Moreover, physics-based approaches often struggle to account for driver behavior, traffic interactions, and environmentalnvariability, which play important roles in determining real-world energy consumption.n    Consequently, while physics-based models provide valuable interpretability and engineering insight, they are often insufficientnwhen applied independently to large-scale transportation environments characterized by complex and rapidly changing operatingnconditions.,

          text     The emergence of machine learning has significantly transformed the field of EV energy prediction. Machine learningnalgorithms are capable of discovering complex nonlinear relationships among variables without requiring explicit mathematicalndescriptions of the underlying physical processes. This capability has made machine learning one of the most widely adoptednapproaches for energy prediction in modern intelligent transportation systems.n    Early machine learning studies utilized linear regression, decision trees, support vector machines, and nearest-neighbornalgorithms to estimate vehicle energy consumption. These methods demonstrated promising results compared with traditionalnanalytical approaches and highlighted the potential of data-driven learning for transportation applications. As computationalnresources and data availability increased, more sophisticated algorithms were introduced to improve predictive performance.n    Ensemble learning methods have become particularly popular in EV energy prediction research. Algorithms such as RandomnForests, Gradient Boosting Machines, XGBoost, and LightGBM combine multiple weak learners to construct highly accuratenpredictive models. These approaches are capable of handling large-scale datasets, nonlinear relationships, and high-dimensionalnfeature spaces while maintaining computational efficiency.n    Among ensemble learning techniques, LightGBM has attracted considerable attention due to its ability to process structuredntabular data efficiently. The algorithm employs gradient-based optimization strategies that reduce computational complexitynwhile maintaining strong predictive performance. Several studies have demonstrated that LightGBM consistently achievesncompetitive accuracy across a variety of transportation and energy forecasting applications.n    Machine learning approaches provide significant advantages over traditional analytical models because they can learn directlynfrom historical vehicle data and adapt to diverse operating environments. Nevertheless, these models often function as black-box,

          text     Deep learning represents a further evolution of data-driven energy prediction methodologies. Unlike traditional machinenlearning algorithms that rely heavily on manually engineered features, deep learning models automatically learn hierarchicalnfeature representations directly from raw data. This capability enables them to capture complex temporal and spatial relationshipsnpresent within transportation datasets.n    Feedforward neural networks were among the earliest deep learning architectures applied to EV energy prediction. Subsequentndevelopments introduced recurrent neural networks, Long Short-Term Memory networks, and Gated Recurrent Units, whichnare particularly effective for modeling sequential driving data. These architectures can capture temporal dependencies amongnvehicle states, battery conditions, and environmental variables, allowing them to model energy consumption patterns over time.n    Deep learning models have demonstrated impressive predictive performance when trained on large datasets. Their abilitynto automatically learn feature representations reduces the need for extensive manual feature engineering and allows them toncapture complex interactions that may be difficult to represent analytically.n    Despite these advantages, deep learning approaches often require substantial computational resources and large quantitiesnof training data. Training procedures may involve extensive hyperparameter tuning and longer computational times comparednwith traditional machine learning algorithms. Furthermore, the lack of interpretability associated with many deep learningnarchitectures remains a significant challenge, particularly in transportation systems where transparency and explainability arenimportant for operational decision-making.n    As a result, researchers have increasingly explored methods that combine the strengths of physical modeling, machinenlearning, and deep learning into unified prediction frameworks.,

          text     The limitations of purely physics-based models and purely data-driven machine learning approaches have motivated thenemergence of Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML). This paradigm seeks to integrate established physical principlesnwith artificial intelligence techniques in order to achieve both predictive accuracy and physical consistency. Rather than treatingnphysical modeling and machine learning as independent methodologies, physics-informed learning combines the strengths ofnboth approaches within a unified framework.n    The fundamental idea behind physics-informed learning is that machine learning models should not rely exclusively onnstatistical correlations present within the training data. Instead, they should be guided by domain knowledge derived fromnscientific principles and engineering theory. In the context of electric vehicle energy prediction, this involves incorporatingnvariables that explicitly represent vehicle dynamics and energy consumption mechanisms.n    Several recent studies have demonstrated that incorporating physics-derived features into machine learning pipelines cannsignificantly improve prediction accuracy. Features such as aerodynamic drag power, rolling resistance power, grade resistancenpower, and inertial power provide physically meaningful representations of vehicle energy demand. Unlike raw telemetrynmeasurements alone, these engineered features directly describe the physical processes responsible for energy consumption.n    Physics-informed models also offer advantages in terms of generalization. Since the learning process is partially constrainednby physical principles, the resulting models are often less susceptible to overfitting and can perform more reliably when exposednto previously unseen operating conditions. This characteristic is particularly important in transportation systems, where drivingnenvironments, weather conditions, and traffic patterns may vary substantially over time.n    Another significant advantage of physics-informed learning is improved interpretability. Transportation engineers and energynresearchers often require an understanding of why a model produces a particular prediction. By incorporating physicallynmeaningful variables into the learning process, physics-informed frameworks provide greater transparency than conventionalnblack-box machine learning approaches.n    Despite these advantages, the application of physics-informed machine learning within electric vehicle energy predictionnremains relatively limited. Most existing studies either focus on purely analytical methods or exclusively data-driven approaches.nConsequently, there remains considerable opportunity to investigate hybrid frameworks that combine vehicle dynamics-basednfeature engineering with modern machine learning algorithms in order to improve both accuracy and interpretability.,

          text     Traditional machine learning approaches rely on centralized training, where data from multiple sources is aggregated withinna single repository before model development. Although centralized learning often achieves strong predictive performance, itnintroduces several practical challenges. Large-scale data transfer increases communication costs, exposes sensitive information,nand creates potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Furthermore, regulatory restrictions may prevent organizations from sharingnraw operational data with external entities.n    Federated Learning has emerged as a promising solution to these challenges. Federated learning enables multiple distributednclients to collaboratively train machine learning models without exchanging raw data. Instead, each client performs localntraining using its own dataset and shares only model parameters, gradients, or aggregated predictions. This approach preservesnprivacy while still allowing knowledge to be extracted from distributed datasets.n    The application of federated learning has expanded rapidly across numerous domains, including healthcare, finance, smartnmanufacturing, and intelligent transportation systems. Within transportation environments, federated learning has been appliednto traffic forecasting, vehicle trajectory prediction, autonomous driving systems, and transportation demand modeling. Thendecentralized nature of transportation data makes federated learning particularly attractive because vehicle information isnnaturally distributed across individual users, fleet operators, charging stations, and geographic regions.n    Several studies have demonstrated that federated learning can achieve predictive performance comparable to centralized learn-ning while significantly reducing privacy risks. However, federated systems introduce new challenges, including communicationnoverhead, client heterogeneity, model synchronization, and computational complexity. Variations in client data distributions cannalso affect convergence and model stability.n    In the context of electric vehicles, federated learning remains an emerging research area. Existing studies have primarilynfocused on battery health estimation, charging demand forecasting, and driver behavior analysis. Comparatively few inves-ntigations have explored federated learning for electric vehicle energy consumption prediction. Furthermore, the integrationnof federated learning with physics-informed feature engineering remains largely unexplored. This observation highlights ansignificant research opportunity for developing privacy-preserving energy prediction frameworks that maintain high levels ofnpredictive accuracy.,

          text     Simulation environments have become indispensable tools for transportation research because they enable controlled ex-nperimentation under realistic traffic conditions. Evaluating predictive algorithms directly in real-world transportation systemsnis often expensive, time-consuming, and operationally challenging. Consequently, researchers frequently employ simulationnplatforms to assess the performance of intelligent transportation technologies before deployment.n    Among available simulation environments, the Simulation of Urban Mobility (SUMO) has emerged as one of the mostnwidely used open-source microscopic traffic simulators. SUMO enables detailed modeling of individual vehicle movements,nroad networks, traffic interactions, traffic control systems, and mobility patterns. The platform supports large-scale transportationnsimulations and has become a standard tool for intelligent transportation research.n    SUMO offers several capabilities that are particularly relevant for electric vehicle studies. Vehicle trajectories, speeds, accel-nerations, traffic densities, route selections, and environmental interactions can all be simulated with high temporal resolution.nThese capabilities allow researchers to evaluate energy consumption models under diverse traffic scenarios and operationalnconditions.n    Recent studies have integrated machine learning techniques with SUMO in order to investigate traffic prediction, congestionnmanagement, route optimization, and autonomous driving systems. For electric vehicle applications, SUMO has been usednto simulate charging behavior, battery usage patterns, energy consumption, and charging infrastructure deployment strategies.nSuch simulations provide valuable insights into how predictive models behave under realistic transportation conditions.n    Despite the widespread use of SUMO, relatively few studies have combined traffic simulation with physics-informed machinenlearning and federated learning frameworks. Most existing simulation-based investigations focus either on transportationnoptimization or machine learning evaluation independently. The integration of advanced predictive models with real-timentransportation simulation therefore represents an important research direction that can bridge the gap between algorithmndevelopment and practical deployment.n    Furthermore, simulation-based evaluation enables researchers to examine system behavior under conditions that may bendifficult or costly to reproduce in real-world environments. As intelligent transportation systems continue to evolve, simulationnplatforms such as SUMO will remain essential tools for validating next-generation energy prediction frameworks.,

          text     The literature reviewed in this section demonstrates significant progress in electric vehicle energy consumption predic-ntion, machine learning, federated learning, and transportation simulation. Nevertheless, several important challenges remainnunresolved.n    First, existing physics-based approaches provide strong interpretability but often struggle to capture the complex nonlinearnrelationships present in real-world transportation systems. Conversely, purely data-driven machine learning approaches achievenhigh predictive performance but frequently lack physical consistency and interpretability. This creates a need for hybridnframeworks capable of combining physical knowledge with machine learning techniques.n    Second, despite the increasing popularity of federated learning, relatively few studies have investigated its application tonelectric vehicle energy consumption prediction. Most existing work focuses on centralized learning architectures that requirenextensive data sharing and raise privacy concerns. The development of privacy-preserving prediction frameworks thereforenremains an important research priority.n    Third, while transportation simulation platforms such as SUMO are widely used for mobility analysis, limited research hasnintegrated physics-informed machine learning models, federated learning architectures, and real-time traffic simulation withinna unified framework. Consequently, the practical deployment readiness of many existing approaches remains uncertain.n    Finally, many existing studies focus exclusively on predictive accuracy while overlooking interpretability, scalability, privacynpreservation, and real-time decision support. Future transportation systems require integrated solutions capable of addressingnall of these requirements simultaneously.n    To address these research gaps, this study proposes a Physics-Informed Federated Learning Framework for Electric VehiclenEnergy Consumption Prediction with Real-Time Traffic Simulation. The proposed framework integrates vehicle dynamics-nbased feature engineering, LightGBM-based prediction, federated learning, SUMO simulation, and dashboard analytics within anunified architecture. By combining these components, the framework aims to achieve high predictive accuracy while maintainingnphysical interpretability, privacy preservation, scalability, and practical deployment readiness.,

          text     To address privacy concerns associated with centralized data collection, the proposed architecture incorporates a federatednlearning framework. The dataset is partitioned according to vehicle identifiers and distributed across twenty federated clients.nEach client performs local model training using only its own subset of vehicle records.n    Rather than sharing raw data, clients contribute local predictive outputs that are combined through weighted aggregation. Thenaggregation weight of each client is proportional to the number of training samples available within that client. This approachnpreserves data privacy while still enabling collaborative model development.n    The federated layer enables the framework to simulate realistic large-scale deployment scenarios where vehicle data remainsndistributed across multiple sources.,

          text     One of the primary limitations of conventional machine learning models is their dependence on statistical relationshipsnextracted directly from data. Although such models often achieve high predictive accuracy, they frequently lack physicalninterpretability and may generate unrealistic predictions when exposed to operating conditions that differ from the trainingndata. In the context of electric vehicle energy consumption prediction, this limitation becomes particularly important becausenvehicle energy demand is fundamentally governed by well-established physical laws.n    To address this challenge, the proposed framework incorporates a Physics-Informed Feature Engineering (PIFE) module. Thenobjective of this module is to augment the original dataset with physically meaningful variables derived from vehicle dynamicsnprinciples. Rather than relying exclusively on raw telemetry measurements, the framework explicitly models the major physicalnforces that contribute to vehicle energy expenditure.n    The resulting physics-informed features provide additional information regarding the underlying mechanisms responsible fornenergy consumption and enable the machine learning model to learn relationships that are both statistically significant andnphysically meaningful.nThe complete feature engineering workflow is illustrated in Fig. 2.,

          text     The rapid growth of connected electric vehicles has resulted in the generation of massive volumes of operational data. Modernnvehicles continuously collect information related to battery performance, driving behavior, environmental conditions, navigationnpatterns, and vehicle dynamics. While these data sources provide valuable opportunities for developing advanced predictivenmodels, they also introduce significant concerns regarding privacy, security, data ownership, and regulatory compliance.n    Traditional machine learning approaches typically rely on centralized training, where data from multiple sources is aggregatedninto a single repository prior to model development. Although centralized learning often achieves strong predictive performance,nit requires extensive data sharing and creates potential privacy risks. In large-scale electric vehicle ecosystems, vehiclenmanufacturers, fleet operators, charging providers, and transportation agencies may be unwilling or unable to share rawnoperational data due to legal, commercial, or privacy-related constraints.n    To address these challenges, the proposed framework incorporates Federated Learning (FL), a distributed machine learningnparadigm that enables collaborative model development without requiring the exchange of raw data. Instead of transferringnvehicle records to a central server, local models are trained independently on distributed datasets, and their outputs are aggregatednto generate a global prediction model.n    The federated learning component of the proposed framework is designed to preserve privacy while maintaining predictivenperformance comparable to centralized learning approaches.,

Several important conclusions can be drawn from the analysis.n    First, vehicle dynamics variables play a critical role in energy prediction.
